lines.text: The Air Force is offering about four thousand seven hundred acres of Alaska for A I data centers.
Some sits at Eielson Air Force Base, outside Fairbanks, where bills are already among the nation's highest.
Does that shrink a Fairbanks bill, or grow it? One number decides. The offering doesn't say.
Nothing's awarded. Alaskans took positions anyway.
Salcha resident Sarah Hollister told reporters the jets always meant sacrifice for freedom.
Swap that for a data center's hum, she said, and we've completely lost our way.
Alaska Senator Lisa Murkowski says the state can't support them on an insecure energy base.
She didn't say the land. She said the power.
Your bill is two things. Wires, and fuel.
The wires split across everyone on the line. Few customers, so that half is tall.
A giant customer helps pay for the wires either way. That half thins.
The fuel is the half that bites. A big load either brings its own power, or competes for what's here.
So it turns on how big. And how big is the number nobody has published.
Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins says defense spending buoyed Fairbanks when the F thirty fives came.
But a fighter wing comes with a budget. A data center comes with an appetite.
So the ask isn't megawatts. Nobody can publish those yet.
Ask for the date. When does that number go public, and is the land leased by then.
The terms aren't written. That's the opening.
